title: The nearest supernova seen since 1604 is lighting up a ring its star shed long before

cover.alt: A glowing ring of bright pink-white spots around a faint purple cloud, the remains of supernova 1987A seen by Hubble.
cover.credit: NASA, ESA, R. Kirshner and P. Challis · CC BY 4.0

body: On 23 February 1987, light from an exploding star in the **Large Magellanic Cloud**, a small galaxy about 168,000 light-years away, reached Earth: the closest supernova seen since Kepler’s in 1604. The star had puffed off rings of gas long before it died; one estimate puts it at 20,000 years earlier. The flash lit the rings briefly, then they faded. Around 2001 the debris of the explosion, moving at more than 7,000 km/s, crashed into the inner ring, and Hubble has watched spot after spot of it light up.

slides.alt: Sequence of Hubble images dated February 1994 to June 2016: an orange ring around a bright centre gains bright spots one by one until the whole ring glows white.
slides.caption: Hubble images from 1994 to 2016, blended in sequence: as the supernova’s debris hits the ring of gas, bright spots appear one by one until the whole ring glows.
slides.credit: NASA, ESA, R. Kirshner and P. Challis · CC BY 4.0 · excerpt

slides.prompt: Something from the explosion reached Earth two to three hours before its light. What was it?
slides.detail: Neutrinos burst out the moment the star’s core collapses. Visible light only escapes later, when the shock wave reaches the star’s surface.

slides.heading: Neutrinos caught from SN 1987A
slides.note: Strictly antineutrinos; 25 in all, out of the vast numbers that passed through Earth

slides.question: Why did the ring around SN 1987A start glowing again years after the explosion?
options: A new star formed in it
slides.explanation: Material thrown out at more than 7,000 km/s caught up with the ring around 2001, heating its gas until it glowed.
